what_its_for: Golimumab is used to treat certain inflammatory conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (a type of spine arthritis), and ulcerative colitis. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation and joint damage. By blocking this protein, golimumab helps reduce pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints and can slow down joint damage over time.
how_to_take: Golimumab comes in two forms: a prefilled autoinjector pen or prefilled syringe that you inject under your skin (subcutaneous injection), usually given once a month; or as an intravenous (IV) infusion given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting. For the self-injection form, common injection sites include your stomach area (abdomen), front of your thighs, or upper outer arms. Rotate injection sites each time and avoid areas that are red, bruised, tender, or hard. Remove the autoinjector from the refrigerator 30 minutes before injecting to let it warm to room temperature. Do not shake the pen or syringe. Always follow the step-by-step instructions provided with your device, and ask your doctor or nurse to show you how to inject correctly before doing it at home.
dosing: The usual dose depends on your condition. For subcutaneous injection (Simponi): the typical adult dose is 50 mg injected under the skin once a month on the same date each month. For rheumatoid arthritis, it is usually taken with methotrexate. For ulcerative colitis, the starting doses are higher (200 mg, then 100 mg two weeks later), followed by 100 mg once a month. For IV infusion (Simponi Aria): doses are given by your healthcare provider in a clinic at weeks 0 and 4, then every 8 weeks. Always take the dose your doctor prescribes — never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss an injection, give it as soon as you remember. Then continue on your regular monthly schedule from the new date. Do not give two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure when to take your next dose after missing one, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store golimumab in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do NOT freeze golimumab — do not use it if it has been frozen. Do not shake the autoinjector or syringe. If needed, you may store the autoinjector or prefilled syringe at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for a single period of up to 30 days, but do not return it to the refrigerator after it has been kept at room temperature. Keep it away from heat and direct sunlight. Safely dispose of used needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine, MMR, chickenpox, or shingles vaccine Zostavax) while taking golimumab, as they may cause serious infections. Talk to your doctor about which vaccines are safe. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially those with active tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B, or other serious infections. Avoid activities that put you at high risk of infection. Do not start golimumab if you currently have any active infection. Tell your doctor before any surgery or dental procedures. Limit alcohol use and discuss any herbal supplements or new medications with your doctor before starting them.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice: signs of infection such as fever, chills, night sweats, cough, shortness of breath, burning when urinating, wounds that won't heal, or unusual tiredness; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat; chest pain or pressure; numbness or tingling in your arms or legs; vision changes; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or new or worsening symptoms of heart failure such as swelling in the ankles or shortness of breath. Also call your doctor before any vaccinations, if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, or if you are scheduled for surgery.
when_it_works: Golimumab may start to relieve symptoms such as pain and swelling within 2 to 4 weeks, but it may take up to 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit. It is important to keep taking it even if you do not feel immediate results. Do not stop taking golimumab without talking to your doctor first, as stopping may cause your symptoms to return.
special_populations: Pregnancy: The safety of golimumab during pregnancy is not fully known. If you took golimumab during pregnancy, your baby should not receive live vaccines for 6 months after birth because the medicine can pass to the baby and affect their immune system. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: It is not known if golimumab passes into breast milk. Discuss with your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Golimumab is approved for use in children 2 years and older for certain conditions such as polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Doses are based on weight. Elderly: Older adults may have a higher risk of infection while taking golimumab. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or Liver Disease: No dose adjustments have been formally established; your doctor will determine if this medication is safe for you.
